opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it started out of convenience and turned into a genuine habit. The big thing for me is long context. I can drop in a whole paper, sometimes the paper plus the appendix plus a couple of related works it's building on, and just have a conversation with all of it at once. I'm not chopping things into pieces or worrying that it lost the thread of section three by the time we get to the experiments.

And the way I use it isn't "summarize this for me." That's the least interesting use. It's more like having a very patient colleague who has read the paper carefully. I'll ask, "What exactly is the baseline here, and is it a fair comparison?" or "Where do they actually define this loss term?" or "Does this result hold up if you look at the ablation table?" It's very good at pointing me to the specific part of the paper, and then I go read that part myself. So it speeds up the critical reading rather than replacing it.

Multimodality matters more than people expect too. A lot of the real content in an ML paper lives in the figures and tables, the scaling plots, the loss curves. Being able to ask about a specific plot, like "what's the slope here" or "why does this curve flatten at that compute budget," is really useful.

There's also a bit of dogfooding in it, to be candid. I work on these models, so using Gemini for something I care about every day is one of the best ways to build intuition for where it's strong and where it still falls short. When it gets something subtly wrong about a paper, that's actually valuable signal for me. So it's partly productivity and partly a constant, informal eval.

r001.rationale: The candidate says they can discuss a whole paper alongside related works it builds on in one conversation.

r002.rationale: It describes critical reading habits, but does not say that greater experience makes readers more demanding about getting directly to key ideas and results.

r003.rationale: The candidate rejects summarization as the main use and says they read the relevant parts themselves; it does not describe extracting essentials to avoid reading the full text when time is limited.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the biggest thing for me is the context window. Research papers aren't short, and when you want to go deep on something, you're often not reading one paper, you're reading a cluster of them. A paper, the two or three it builds on, maybe an appendix that's forty pages of ablations. With Gemini I can just drop all of that in at once and have the whole thing in context, and then ask questions that cut across them. "How does the training recipe here differ from the one in this other paper?" "Is this claim actually supported by the numbers in table three?" That kind of cross-referencing is exactly the thing that's tedious to do by hand and exactly the thing the model is good at when it can actually see everything.

The second thing is that it's multimodal in a way that really matters for papers. So much of the information in a paper lives in the figures and the plots, not the prose. Being able to point at a scaling curve or an architecture diagram and ask "what's going on here" and get a sensible answer changes how fast I can get the gist of something.

And then I should be honest that there's a bias here. I work on Gemini, so part of it is that I want to use the thing we're building, I want to feel where it's strong and where it breaks. Reading papers is a great test case for that because I usually know the material well enough to catch it when it's confidently wrong. So it's partly a tool and partly an ongoing evaluation. But I'd say the long context plus the ability to reason over figures is genuinely what makes it my default, not just loyalty.

astra-6.text: For me, it’s the ability to put the whole paper into the context and have a conversation about it. When I’m reading something dense, I want to ask, “What’s the intuition behind this?” or “How does this equation connect to the claim they’re making?” And then keep digging into whichever part I don’t understand. Gemini works well for that workflow. I still want to check the actual paper, but having something to talk it through with makes the process much easier.

sol-6.1.text: For me, the big advantage is being able to put the whole paper into the context and have a conversation about it. I can ask for the main argument, dig into an equation, or ask how a particular experiment supports the conclusion, without having to break the paper into little pieces. That makes it useful as a reading companion. I still want to check the paper myself, but it helps me get oriented and work through the parts I don’t immediately understand.
